text:
emily.s: Quick architecture question — for Private customer VPCs should we push for per-customer egress proxies (sidecar or shared per-account proxy) or lean on a central NAT/egress VPC that they route to? Trying to weigh security/zoning vs cost/operational complexity.
raj.k: Short answer: tradeoffs. Per-customer egress = stronger isolation and easier per-tenant audit, but higher cost and ops surface. Central NAT = cheaper but more blast radius.
sofia: Also consider transit limits and routing complexity. Central NAT via TGW or Transit VPC can create transitive routing needs if we do peering + egress in another account.
luis: Is the control plane still fully separated? If control plane endpoints are PrivateLink into customer VPCs we can keep control-plane traffic inbound-only and avoid egress for control plane. That reduces need for customer-wide egress controls.
emily.s: Yes control plane = inbound PrivateLink + webhook callbacks over a dedicated peering path. But customer apps (LLM calls to model endpoints) may still need internet egress for model pulls, metrics, third-party telemetry.
sofia: For those, we could propose a hybrid pattern: mandatory minimal egress allowlist (S3/ECR/KMS/metrics) via VPC endpoints + optional central NAT for everything else. That way most heavy traffic stays private.
raj.k: Agreed. Operationally we can automate endpoint provisioning with the onboarding flow and put a stray-folder for edge cases. Also watch for hairpinning if the central egress sits in a different AZ/account — adds latency.
luis: Practical note: AWS VPC peering doesn't support transitive routing; if we use per-region TGW we can avoid full mesh but TGW adds cost. For small customers, per-account sidecar proxy (tiny t3/t4g) might be cheapest.
sofia: Security tradeoff: central NAT requires us to manage egress filtering centrally (badged rules, SIEM integration). Sidecars push policy to customer boundary — better zero-trust alignment.
emily.s: How about operational templates? Proposed options for onboarding: 1) Minimal-private: VPC endpoints only (free-ish) 2) Shared-eager: TGW + central NAT 3) Isolated: per-customer egress proxy + optional ILB. Thoughts on defaults?
raj.k: Default to 1) minimal-private. If customer requests SLAs/dedicated throughput -> 2). If they insist on isolation + compliance -> 3). Keep migration path.
sofia: We should document fallback behavior in the console: if central egress exhausted, control plane should route to a lower-throughput model variant (same as our runtime fallbacks). Make sure that is surfaced.
luis: Implementation nit: provisioning script for endpoints + route-table change snippet for onboarding: ```bash
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-id $VPC --service-name com.amazonaws.$REGION.s3 --route-table-ids rtb-...
aws ec2 replace-route --route-table-id rtb-xxx --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --nat-gateway-id nat-xxx
```
emily.s: Nice. Who wants to follow up with an RFC-style doc for this hybrid onboarding flow? Include cost estimates (NAT per-hour vs sidecar EC2 cost) and failure modes.
sofia: I'll draft the RFC; include sample diagrams for TGW vs PrivateLink topologies and a quick checklist for compliance customers.
raj.k: I'll pull recent cost numbers and a small simulator for expected egress GB/month per customer so we can recommend defaults.
infra-bot: Reminder: tagging required labels: #networking #private-deployments #onboarding (auto).
luis: :thumbsup: sounds good. emily.s — can you create the RFC issue and assign sofia + raj?
emily.s: Yup creating now, will link back here. Thanks everyone :raised_hands:
